title: SYSK Selects: How Crack Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "How Crack Works," chosen by Josh. The hosts explain how crack is made from cocaine (baking soda or ammonia, boiling) versus freebasing with ether, and how it affects dopamine reuptake in the brain, producing a short, intense, highly addictive high. They cover health risks (heart attack, stroke, cocaine-alcohol byproduct cocaethylene), withdrawal and treatment (including contingency management), and street slang. Much of the episode covers history: the 1980s crack epidemic, the Contra war and allegations of CIA involvement via Freeway Ricky Ross and Gary Webb's Dark Alliance series and the press backlash against Webb, the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act and drug-law racism, the 100-to-1 crack/cocaine sentencing disparity and the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010, the crack baby myth and the later study finding poverty and postnatal care mattered more, and the rise of modern gangs. The episode closes with a listener email about PTSD after a police chase.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, How Crack Works, and the hosts trade banter about 'whack' and related jokes before the main topic.

segments.title: Cocaine and the 1980s crack epidemic
segments.summary: The hosts describe cocaine's expense and upscale image in the early 1980s, then the cheaper crack that spread through lower-income African American areas, and Nancy Reagan's anti-drug response.

segments.title: Nicaragua, the Contras, and CIA drug allegations
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Sandinista revolution and US support for the Contras, and the allegations that CIA-linked groups sold cocaine to Freeway Ricky Ross. They cite the Kerry/Carey committee findings and a later CIA internal investigation, which found no evidence the CIA itself brought drugs into the US but did not cut ties with some alleged traffickers.

segments.title: Gary Webb and the Dark Alliance backlash
segments.summary: Gary Webb's Dark Alliance series linked the CIA-backed Nicaraguan group to Freeway Ricky Ross. The hosts describe the rebuttals from major newspapers, Webb's later career decline and death, and an upcoming film.

segments.title: History of cocaine and the Harrison Act
segments.summary: The hosts trace cocaine's isolation in the mid-1800s, its popularity in tonics and as a prescription drug, and its criminalization under the 1914 Harrison Narcotics Tax Act, which they tie to racist fears.

segments.title: How crack is made and freebasing
segments.summary: The hosts explain making cocaine powder from coca paste, freebasing with ether, and how crack is made by boiling cocaine with baking soda or ammonia. They discuss Richard Pryor's freebasing accident and the name crack from its crackling sound, plus crack pipes.

segments.title: Dopamine, the crack high, and health effects
segments.summary: The hosts explain how crack blocks dopamine reuptake, producing a short, intense high that drives addiction, then cover physical risks including heart attack, stroke, and the liver-toxic cocaethylene formed when mixed with alcohol.

segments.title: Withdrawal, treatment, and street slang
segments.summary: The hosts describe crack withdrawal symptoms, the lack of medication, behavioral therapy and contingency management, and a list of street names for crack.

segments.title: Crack sentencing disparity and the Fair Sentencing Act
segments.summary: The hosts explain the 100-to-1 powder-to-crack sentencing ratio, the five-year mandatory minimum for possession, the 2010 Fair Sentencing Act that changed the ratio to 18-to-1, and retroactive releases.

segments.title: Crack baby myth
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1980s crack baby panic, the predicted lost generation, and a later study that found poverty and postnatal care, not prenatal crack exposure alone, explained the lower outcomes. They note alcohol's greater harm in pregnancy.

segments.title: Gangs and the crack trade
segments.summary: The hosts say the crack trade helped the rise of modern inner-city gangs such as the Crips, Bloods, and Folks, because crack was easy to sell and control.

segments.title: Listener mail: police chase and PTSD
segments.summary: Rebecca shares that she was hit by teens fleeing police in a high-speed chase, developed PTSD and anxiety, and got treatment; she argues police should weigh the risk of chases for minor crimes.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: The hosts recap the episode's topics and sign off, with a reminder on how to contact the show.
